item.title: Some Problems
item.content:encoded:
I recommend you try posting to the sandbox website, it is specifically designed to receive criticism and help you improve the SCP before posting. Even experienced writers use the sandbox a lot and make tons of edits before they post their SCP here. Also if you haven't read through this page yet I recommend to do so. http://www.scpwiki.com/how-to-write-an-scp Now on to my personal thoughts of this SCP. There is a lot wrong with this, but there is also a lot of potential. For starters the photo is in the wrong place, and the interview log isn't properly formatted. To fix these you should reread the formatting section of the "How to Write an SCP" page. Secondly there are some more subtle errors, like how the containment box is 5x5 when it should be 5x5x5. But all of that can be fixed with some minor editing. A bigger problem is why the interview log is included. It doesn't tell us anything new except for explain how the effects were discovered, and that's just a little boring. Either change what the interview is about or cut it entirely. By far the biggest problem with this SCP is that there isn't anything particularly weird or scary about it. It would be more interesting if, for example, it did more than just erase memories. Like maybe it could give you fake memories, or if it slowly made you lose all of your memories. Just something to make the reader think about it after they've finished reading.

item.title: Alternative Classification System (Seeking Greenlight)
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article (potentially -J if idea is decided to be too silly/meta by reviewers)

Genre (Optional): Comedy

Elevator Pitch:
+ show block
– hide block

A connection on the internal Foundation database with unknown source that leads to a database of documented SCP Objects that is mostly identical to foundation's own, with key difference being that classification system used for SCP types is different. Connection severs itself and immedeately reinstates every 24 hours, connecting to a different alternative database. In addition to that, any attempt at documenting the SCP itself results in it changing its own classification to match whatever system is used in current connection.

Central Narrative:
+ show block
– hide block

The connection is direct and two-way, but read-only veiw into a tiny glimpse of life of Foundation in alternate reality. Due to nature of the SCP all realities remain the same in terms of amount of knowledge on SCPs themselves and state of foundation, with extremely rare exceptions. However, differences in things unrelated to SCPs themselves are fairly common, if hard to find due to nature of the materials being accessed. In addition, all the access restrictions are still perfectly functional, so researcher in charge of the SCP cannot access any particularly classified one without direct permission. Through continuous observation, Foundation also finds very minor ways to enchance its performance, though again, in fields unrelated to the handling or finding SCPs themselves.

Hook/Attention-Grabber:
+ show block
– hide block

Primarily, the article would be a list of various alternative systems of classification recorded, ranging from reasonable to completely absurd to downright esoteric. Regular notes about differences that aren't the system itself would also allow it to not be excessively repetitive.

Additional Notes:
+ show block
– hide block

The focus will mostly be lighthearted moreso than comedic, if it is approved as regular article. Main inspiration for the article has been growth of use of esoteric SCP Classes in recent articles, and its meant to be a light little meta reference to that, while still being reasonable as a standalone thing.

item.title: Re: I LOVE the lolfoundation
item.content:encoded:
Well, everyone doesn't "have a problem" with it, they just don't like when it intrudes on works intended to be serious. lolfoundation has its own separate canon so all the wacky shenanigans can take place over there without intruding on the supreme horror of the 3000-contest entries or what have you. Articles written to create more of a serious tone are completely ruined by things like demotion to D-class and wacky addenda, which break most people's suspension of belief because an organization like the Foundation wouldn't really be so careless. In general, I think most of the website's users come here for horror, which doesn't mesh great with wacky shenanigans. Like I said, though, there's a whole separate canon for lolfoundation. There aren't a whole lot of comparable shenanigans going on in most mainlist articles, but a few gems like SCP-4444 and SCP-5004 do still feature the senior staff being funny. Also, the Resurrection canon also has some elements of lolfoundation in it - Duke 'til Dawn and Incident 239-B really happened in Resurrection, and comparable things (within reason) can still happen to an extent.

tl;dr funny Foundation is still a thing, it's just separated out from regular Foundation more than it used to be.

item.title: Re: SCP Concept: Reflection
item.content:encoded:
Hey there Cesss, I'll be critting your idea today!
Note that I am not a particularly experienced nor official reviewer (like the others here), so take what I say with a grain of salt. With that being said, let's begin the crit!

+ Open Section-by-Section +
- Close Section-by-Section -

Elevator Pitch

I'm going to be honest, I don't really like this idea. All it is is a random gas station that, for some reason, has mirrors that cause your reflection to take control of you and then kill you. Why? Are the reflections like some kind of demon or something? This just seems like a less interesting/creative version of SCP-919, which presents a moral/ethical dilemma over whether the reflections are animate or not, rather than a reflection that just kills you.

Central Narrative

This narrative is… adequate, but I still don't like the concept behind it. It just isn't interesting enough for me to have a random gas station mirror with murderous, possessive reflections. There is also a logistical problem behind your narrative: how did the Foundation find this footage? Unless there was a camera on the Researcher's body (extremely unlikely), there is no way they could have information this detailed on the Researcher's death.

Hook/Attention Grabber

So the gas station moves and people start swapping consciousnesses their own reflections. That's it. The swapping part could be interesting if explored more, but the gas station (and the fact that it moves) seems… disjointed. Why are the reflections part of a gas station? Why does the gas station move?

+ Open General Thoughts +
- Close General Thoughts -

At the moment, your idea would likely be downvoted by members of this Site (myself included) if it became an article, mostly due to a lack of substance. This lack of substance takes the form of:
- A boring/uncreative anomaly
- Little story
- The slightly disjointed/random nature of the separate parts of the anomaly
- The fact it is a 'thing that kills you' SCP (a common trope on this Site, whereby the anomaly is simply something that kills you without much backstory or substance)
Simply put, this idea isn't interesting enough. All it is a killer reflection in a random, moving gas station. Now, if this were reflections trying to take over their 'real' counterparts (i.e switch bodies with them) and having identity crises, I'd be interested. Hearing the tale of a scientist who lost their body and gained it back after hunting their eisoptrophobic (afraid of mirrors) reflection and cornering them in a room with a mirror (idk, that's just a story I came up with. You can use it, if you want) is interesting to me. As it stands, this is just effectively an anomalous murderer. The end.

I'd recommend two things:
1. Check out the Guide Hub for some great ideation/narrative creation advice!
2. Contact reviewers from the Butterfly Squad to get some experienced alternative opinions!

And finally, to sum up your idea in one sentence1:
Moving gas station has mirrors which cause your reflection to possess you and make you kill yourself.

Just some things for you to reflect on.


Anyway, that's about it for my crit today. Thanks for reading, and hopefully this helps!
Footnotes
1. This is to assist you in getting a quick, outside view of your idea, which may help you change something you might have missed/you don't like about your own idea.

Forum thread: SCP-INTEGER

This article has a solid core. There is something quite enchanting about the simplicity of 'a guy chasing you'. I like how the German is characterised by how he changes over time - there is a subtle dread to knowing that he is improving his craft. I really appreciate that the excerpts of the book are not told from his perspective - just a little drip of characterisation every now and then was enough.

Beyond the core, though, things are a little lacking. I wish it had been a little clearer in-universe on why those book excerpts were worth attaching. I found the excerpts from the journal unsatisfying. The points they introduced felt too convenient for cheap character development - not unforgivable, seeing as they are excerpts after all - but to me they didn't feel like entries of a journal. The decline was far too linear for excerpts taken more than 100 days apart. It's fine that this was used to explain why the character failed in their task, but it would have been a good opportunity for passive characterisation of the German.

I am tired of "oh no! it got worse!" as a cliffhanger. I don't feel like I've gained anything by knowing that there is undeveloped plot, and I don't think it's worth the confusion at the start of trying to decide whether or not I care about reading the previous conprocs/desc or if I just want to get into the flow of the article. There's also a divergence that I'd've liked to have seen developed. A lot of stuff happens during the dream described as if it happens in the real world. I'd like to know what actually happened.

Novote overall.

item.title: Re: Roadless Trip
item.content:encoded:
Starting 'er up...
Nevermind, they're watching

Ok, so as of right now, I'm thinking that the car (or rather, our resident suited fellow) will refuse to leave if being directly observed or recorded visually. It is, however, possible to track the car with something like GPS, and even possible to record audio on or around the car, in which case the sounds that would be recorded could include: the engine revving up, the car peeling out, sounds from the cars immediate environment but never including collision despite the cars route. I hadn't considered GPS till reading your message about cameras. GPS would just show the car taking a straight path to it's destination. I'm still mulling over whether I think the suited man would leave the devices planted on the car be longer than one trip, having subsequent trips begin with the removal of said devices.

I'm very glad to hear the foundation would be game for testing the anomalous properties despite their including the car leaving temporarily. This makes things much easier. I think that once the foundation has a better grasp of how the car works, it will be easy to contain, only really needing surveillance, which will keep it where it is 99% of the time (I'm planning on having a single log where video footage cuts out suddenly, and the cameras to the car's containment being damaged). The majority of logs will be either before the foundation has a grasp of what is going on, and in tests where they intend to try to control the situation to the best of their ability.

Where do I go from here? Maybe its selfish to be asking you because I feel like there is probably a guide on this somewhere, but I'm still trying to understand this all. Is this the stage where I start actually writing the logs and article? Do I just need to be able to explain my idea in a more solid way? I know there will be more steps before its done (obviously) but I'm not 100% certain of what my current step is.

Again, thank you for the feedback. I really mean it. I feel like I have trouble taking criticism sometimes, and am trying to get over that flaw of mine, but I haven't had any issues with that yet. I feel like your input has brought me much closer to understanding my own SCP, and has guided the way I've looked at this project. So thanks

item.title: Re: Forum Criticism Team - Captain Post
item.content:encoded:
What if I, for example, change them into two separate entities? Would that change the concept from the status quo?

No, because you fundamentally still have a cliche rage-state humanoid (tacking on the 073/076 reference worsens the situation, since then you have a cliche rage state humanoid with a gratuitous namedrop reference to a popular article from over a decade ago—readers often interpret that as an attempt to draw attention via referencing someone else's work, and it feels more like unnecessary shoehorning, not so much interesting worldbuilding).

If you really want to keep the rage state setup, you'll need to add more to the character (ideally, without referencing other SCP articles) so they're not solely defined by that trope. What you have currently feels like a slight rehash of Persephone/Kore as portrayed by the webcomic Lore Olympus. Readers have seen this sort of approach attempted many times before on the mainsite and many times in popular media. If all you have to the entity is their rage ability, they're going to seem more like a generic one-dimensional OC rather than a believable individual that the average reader will care about enough to read about.

What is unique to your character that isn't reliant on other authors' work? How is this character relatable to the average very human, very not magical reader? What is the history of the entity and how will that make readers care about them?

item.title: Re: Slimy Science about Acids
item.content:encoded:
I apologize for the very extensive response. I found it very difficult to say everything I wanted to say as concisely as possible, so I would recommend skipping down to the final paragraph for a very quick summary of everything I mentioned in the following paragraphs which have been collapsed for your convenience.

+Open
+Close

I realize that the central narrative is very lacking, and I don't really want to focus on a horror focused narrative either. I doubt I would be able to capture the anxiety I experienced when I dreamed about a green acid that could dissolve everything except plastic and could quickly become a tsunami of acid in mere minutes. (As a side note, even if I could capture that anxiety in writing that dream happened when I was much younger and reflecting back on the dream makes me feel silly how it made me so anxious.)

I realize that figuring out what emotion or thought I want to create in readers is very important when writing a central narrative, and I would rather have the reader to think about the implications of what they are reading. While acidic slime is a strange idea in general, I would say that the slime being unable to dissolve plastic would add to the strangeness. I want readers to think and wonder why the slime can dissolve stainless steel but not plastic. Providing theories about the reasons behind the slime's inability to dissolve plastic by the Foundation researchers is meant to get readers to think and even possibly make up their own theories on the reason. While I understand all of this would not be very compelling and would not garner much reader retention, I feel like the idea would work best in this way.

Regardless, I have been brainstorming and trying to come up with a much better central narrative to tell, but I've run into a few problems in my thought processes. While I could write a story of how the Foundation discovered the slime, I would be more inclined to say that the Foundation discovered it as it was destroying a large area which would make things very difficult when taking into account that the slime's volume increases as it dissolves materials. As a result, it would be extremely difficult to explain how the Foundation was able to trap the slime because the amount of slime could fairly easily cover at least half of an entire suburban area by the time the Foundation could work against it, and even then the Foundation would have to discover the slime's inability to dissolve plastic. To summarize, the slime would very likely already cover such a vast area that completely surrounding it with plastic would be almost impossible to achieve. While I could say that the Foundation happened upon the slime and quickly discovered its anomalous properties as part of the central narrative, it is unlikely to be compelling.

Another idea I have thought about was the possibility of a researcher accidentally dropping a bit of slime on an area not covered by plastic allowing the slime to begin dissolving the Site, but I am afraid I would be too inclined to make the slime dissolve a large area of the Site which would in turn be affected by the flaws of the first idea I mentioned in the previous paragraph while also creating the notion that it would be endangering almost all of the SCPs contained in the Site to such a scale that the SCP Foundation could potentially lose numerous SCPs entirely due to the SCPs getting dissolved. While I could avoid that and write about the Foundation being able to quickly avoid the previously mentioned scenario by removing the slime from the affected area before it becomes virtually impossible to contain, that notion does not sound very appealing to me, and I feel like it would not add very much either.

I believe I've seen a Wondertainment science kit before

The Wondertainment science kit you are thinking of is SCP-1224. I had previously checked and looked at all of the SCPs associated with Wondertainment before creating this thread, and I am concerned that making the slime as part of a science kit would be too similar to SCP-1224.

Originally, the concept was just a jar full of acidic slime made by Wondertainment; however, I realized it would be difficult to "justify" the reasoning behind the slime being acidic if it was just a jar full of acidic slime. I decided to make it part of a science kit about acids that was centered around slime in particular because I felt that made much more sense and gave a much more practical reasoning behind the slime being acidic. Doing so also allowed me to explore the notion that Wondertainment knew how dangerous the slime was and still decided to make it public for children to play with anyway by providing plastic gloves, goggles, a sheet, and even a lab apron for the children to "safely" handle the slime. However, I will look into other "pseudo child education tools" because I would like to make this concept as polished as possible.

To summarize, I realize the central narrative is the main issue for this concept. However, I feel like the concept would work better if it was written in a way to get readers to think about the idea of acidic slime, so that the strangeness of the idea can garner some interest in the reader to continue reading. Also, I want to intrigue readers as they read instead of trying to make the slime scary or more in the horror genre. Sadly, I have had some struggles in trying to spice up the central narrative to make it more interesting as many of my ideas do not sound very practical when considering the implications of the slime's abilities. Furthermore, I am concerned that the concept is too similar to SCP-1224 since both are Wondertainment science kits, but I felt that the concept worked much better as a science kit than just a jar full of acidic slime while also giving me a little bit of creative freedom to explore a more interesting notion; however, I will take your advice and look into other "pseudo child education tools."

I hope that I was at least able to give you an idea of my thought process and the direction I would like to take this concept. I also realize that this response makes the notion of this idea being too "overdone" much more pronounced. Again, I apologize for this very extensive reply.

item.title: Re: The "Uncontainable" SCP
item.content:encoded:
+ Response
– hide block

In an old audio log found by the foundation, during questioning for why he wants to join the spirit, they ask him why he wants to join them.

Hmm, here's a word of advice about audio logs like this: You're gonna want to use them to really emphasize this character's personality and vernacular by contrast. Ideally, since he's a bad guy at this point in the narrative, he should be fairly abrasive to Foundation personnel but you're gonna have to juggle that with seeing him be endearing.

I could have a video feed cut out, but the audio would still be there, this would be where I would put the audio log, which by what your saying, I assume is actually recorded by me.

This log things sounds good, but there's no need to record audio like that, you can just write it out.

As for highlighting the attempts, which I assume you mean are the crimes, I could have a log of all the actions he does like this

I struggle a bit with crit like this, since I don't want to infringe upon authorial intent, but I was thinking more along the lines of an addendum with a brief description of what he did, followed by a panicked phone call between him and the Foundation as he's locking himself in the back of the store after being overwhelmed by the police presence.

The reason I recommend this approach is because it's just a better setting for character growth and revelation — you've got two parties in a high-stakes environment, one of which is attempting to swallow his pride enough to ask the other for help. The stakes and the interaction tend to produce more dynamic characters than a simple timeline.

So I think I'm getting a better understanding of how this is shaping up, and I think this is gonna be the most solid narrative we've devised so far.

  1. Dude joins the Spirit, makes some connections, eventually falls into the Foundation's pocket after their disbandment due to him being incompetent without backup.
  2. He has an intake interview where his character is established to the reader and some of his backstory is illuminated.
  3. In an effort to mitigate future containment breaches, the Foundation positions him in a heavily-monitored janitorial position with some promise of upward mobility.
  4. A combination of pride and an itch in his gut leads him to breach containment, attempting to pull off a crime to prove he's really a criminal after all; this goes south and he requests re-containment by the Foundation.
  5. Following re-containment he is approached by one of his old contacts in the Spectre who offers him a way back to his old life; he comes close to taking the deal but some unspecified thing that's occurred in the narrative previously compels him to reject the offer — maybe he realizes that his past wasn't anything he should be chasing after.1
  6. He eventually works his way back up to a senior position on the janitorial staff.

Does that generally sound like a story you want to go after?

Footnotes
1. I'm specifically imagining a part of the phone conversation where the Foundation asks if he used his anomalous ability to hurt anyone and he says he doesn't do that anymore and seems horrified.

Excellent, excellent; thank you for clarifying. This is shaping up real well.

Responding to a conversation that occurred in PMs, I still believe the "middle" of the story you've got is a little lacking. Ideally you would want to fill it with primary evidence taken from the premises of her previous holders, such as a convenient journal entry (either documenting someone's personal thoughts or, more ideally, "containment procedures" and incident reports). This could be followed by a Foundation incident report of some kind, which would highlight the malevolent intent of the reflections.

I also still take issue with this end-of-article twist being revealed in an interview room, given upon being asked for it nicely. There should be something in the way of the audience learning this information that, when it's overcome, is satisfying. I'd imagine this would be as simple as having her be non-responsive to questioning, and then reveals the information to a researcher after some big event occurs (that aforementioned incident report, perhaps?). I'm imagining a scene of the girl and a researcher standing in front of a mirror in her containment chamber, when she suddenly begins to speak to them — the imagery, at least, is more varied than a mundane interview room.

This execution would require you to really nail the feeling of dread that should be emanating from these reflection people, to make them seem like a good thread. Does any of that sound interesting?

item.title: Re: Irish Fairies

Gotta start off by saying, I’m generally a fan of all things fae (I mean, just look at my profile picture). So I like the idea of a fairy-based SCP. Though I’m noticing a few things here that I have to question.

First, what’s with the symmetrical hole? It just seems random and it’s never really explained. You seem to have such a consistent them with the traits later, and then there’s just this at the beginning. Second, is this actually fairies or is it just fairy-like? Either answer is fine but you want your reader to understand which it is. Because if I were reading this I’d think “cool, a forest that makes people go insane” not “there are probably creatures in that forest”. So if you actually want to be using fairies you should probably have some appear, but if you just want to use the traits of fairies and attribute them to a forest that’s also an option.

I’m going to throw out a suggestion, and keep in mind that you by no means have to take this. But you might want to write this as a tale. After all it doesn’t seem like you’re that interested in the containment of this anomaly. You didn’t even touch on that in your pitch. I could see a tale that was entirely devoted to the task force exploring this forest. It would give us more of a view into how they’re reacting to all the chaos happening around them. Again, I’m just throwing that out there. This can still work perfectly fine as a regular article.

item.title: Re: So Let It Be Written, So Let It Be Done
item.content:encoded:
Thanks for the Feedback
Hide Reply

Thanks, Dankaar,

I appreciate the feedback, first and foremost. The reverse approach, seeing the unaffected astronauts as the affected, is fascinating. Lots of potential for "containment" by keeping an eye on earth-bound events by comparing them to a non-earth-bound control.

In my drafts, neither of the original holders of the stone ever realize that the stone is the cause of the anomalous events. With all the tools that are used, the new location, the impracticality of testing individual books and tools, they're simply unable to pinpoint the source. Hence the frustration and the eventual unravelling of their characters.

Also, in my drafts (I'm writing this story out long form for NaNoWriMo), the SCP's effects are limited to the event itself (raising Atlantis from a repaired book on Greek Mythology), and public perception of the event. Centuries of evidence concluding that Atlantis was an allegory invented by Plato to make a point still exist unchanged. People can and occasionally do come across this evidence but, as the ultimate confirmation bias, they assume that it's all flawed or incorrect because they just know the place is real. In the long form, the protagonists realize that they know both realities are true before remembering that they'd set up a test to change a particular outcome. The SCP doesn't rewrite history, really, it just changes our perception of it, and so the physical changes are accepted as reality.

I too was struggling with how the Foundation gets in on this, but I really love the "reverse effect" perspective which alerts them to Foundation-level weirdness, after which they trace the effects back to stone… somehow. I was tempted to throw an MC&D reference in with the antique store, perhaps the Foundation was tracking this artifact without knowing its effects, and the investigations merge.

Thank you again for the feedback and ideas!

item.title: Re: the man in the corner
item.content:encoded:
DISCLAIMER: I am a newbie and I cannot give green-lights.

Please take everything I say with a grain of salt

This is a placeholder, I will give my thoughts on this as soon as I can

So besides some grammer and formatting issues which I'm sure some others shall go over, I'll go ahead and tell you what I really enjoy about the SCP and what I'm really confused about it.

What I like about this concept

1. It's an interesting concept. An old man who ensures his captivity area is perfectly smooth via the use of shadows is definitely a new concept. One that can adapt to his environment and understand the humans around him is definitely an interesting trait. I also enjoy the use of shadows.

READ MORE
READ LESS

What I'm confused about or dislike about this concept

So there's quite a bit I'm confused about. I definitely believe you need to flesh out the story and SCP idea in-general. I recommend spending more time on your SCP concept and think "how does this pertain to the story I'm trying to tell?", "how does this tell us about the Foundation?", and "what seems to be missing?".

The biggest advice I can give you is that the concept overall needs to be refined

except he is always facing the corner of a room facing magnetic north at midnight and every two hours moves to another corner.

1. How does he face the corner of a room he's in if he faces the magnetic north? In my opinion, I don't believe the changing of corners or facing magnetic north needs to be added here as it doesn't pertain to your central narrative you are trying to tell.

His face is always in shadow nothing can be done to see it or probe it

2. How is his face always in shadow? Does he somehow have something covering his face? I'm not necessarily sure what you meant by this.

He must always be kept in a perfectly square room made of concrete with an aggregate of bone and seashell one of the few objects he cannot destroy.

3. Why is this? I understand he can't destroy those materials, but it is never explained that the SCP destroys the room.

The SCP does this by creating a black shadow around itself that engulfs the room no light can enter this shadow and any who enter are turned to bone and blood.

3. This might be a bit petty but I don't think that's a shadow. A shadow is emitted via the use of light and an object blocking the light from reaching a surface. This seems more like a aura or "circular radius".

The walls must be perfectly smooth any cracks or chips in the wall causes the SCP to react and turn the room back to a perfect square.

4. Do the walls normally become cracked? The SCP seems to already make sure that his room is as smooth as butter when it comes to cracks and chips. There seems to be no reason for this to be one of the things the Foundation has to look out for. I believe this is a simple misunderstanding of what you're trying to say.

I believe you're trying to say "if the room the SCP is contained in has any imperfection around it, such as an object or crack in the wall, it will cause the SCP to react…"

The initial discovery of the SCP in Canada comes first along with a new mobile task force called the Canada goose.

4. Why the need for a new mobile task force? In my opinion, I don't believe there is a need for one. Also I recommend giving more detail into your SCP's discovery.

The next is an incident involving a chip in the wall and the SCP’s reaction then two files hidden by 05 council. Then a new test which gives a hint to removed files and finally placing the SCP in a perfectly round room.

5. Although I like the idea you're going for, why hide the files? If the files are supposed to be hidden for no one besides the O5-council (meaning that it is EXTREMELY HIDDEN) then it shouldn't be referenced afterwards in the following file? I recommend not adding this in. It could work, but needs some rethinking.

The next is an incident involving a chip in the wall

6. Where are these chips coming from? Are they coming from the SCP? If the chip on the wall makes the SCP enact dangerous actions, explain that the Foundation is trying to ensure these "chips in the wall" don't occur.

There is more to the SCP than what we see it is hinted he knows foundation secrets.

7. This isn't well explained enough. How do we know the SCP knows more than what he sees? Does he explain it in some way?

An old man

8. So it's a humanoid SCP. Does he talk in some way? How does him being "an old man" relate to how he acts or how the story is? Remember he technically acts like a human since he's an old man. Read here for more about writing humanoid SCPs in the "Humanoids" tab: http://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/how-to-write-an-scp

The initial discovery

9. Ok so, how does the SCP react when it's outside and not in a corner? If it's never been out of a corner because it's impossible, how did the Foundation manage to contain the SCP? Where was he located in the first place? Try to give more detail in this.

Overall, its definitely an idea I think you could make work, but it definitely needs a lot of rework and re-evaluation to ensure the concept given is solid before asking for critique. Remember, don't let these comments discourage you, and try to take the criticism you get as a way to improve your concept.

Good luck to you, feel free to PM on wikidot and I'll gladly come back to see your idea once you feel that you reworked it enough. :)

he is always facing the corner of a room facing magnetic north at midnight

bone and seashell one of the few objects he cannot destroy.

Then… he can destroy everything else? Why is precisely bone and seashell the things that he cannot destroy? I'm feeling like you're trying to give the man too many powers and abilities. Maybe it would be better to keep the anomaly within the creepiness of a guy always facing a corner.

So, my question is this: does this SCP affect the relevant records on Earth anytime the SCP does its thing?

If so, you could attack this from the opposite angle: the SCP Foundation initially belives the SCP to be an event that affects sattleites and astronauts, ocasionally implanting both with fake memories or data about Earth, when what is really happening is the stone thing. The sattleites and astronauts are unaffected because the effects of the SCP are strictly Earthbound.

From there, you could then work your way to the narrative you had planned (perhaps the SCP being from a seperate investigation initially unrelated to the sattleite phenomenon?) I suggest this because, as-is, it would be difficult for the Foundation to "naturally" learn of this SCP's existence, and you've kinda-sorta created a plot hole by having the book binders suspect that the SCP is causing the stuff despite its effects on humanity's perception of history. Having them chase down the effects (even if they're incorrect) feels like a better way.

Also burning the bookstore in-universe is a bit much if the intent was to destroy the SCP. Sledgehammer or dropping it from a high place would've been the smater move for the guys.

Thank you for giving me the opportunity to clarify my stance, which I will do now: This is 100% NOT supposed to be a "haha boob" joke. I now understand how my juxtaposition of the word "comedy" with this piece (which is, indeed, intended to be an anti-harassment tale) caused confusion; the part that I viewed as humorous was the fate of the lecher who, as a result of his inability to quit ogling, was ultimately forced to do so.

A detail I omitted from my brief description that perhaps would have helped me better express my true intentions, one which I do plan to include in the finished piece, should I write it, is that during experimentation, the carved possessive word which seemingly appears on her body is observed to come from no one and nowhere but the SCP itself (i.e. there is no "other being" out there causing it): it is an act of self-claiming, of saying "Lay off; this isn't yours to stare at".

Speaking of testing, almost all of the test data and containment procedure will, of course, be conducted with Dr. Lopez's full consent and within her comfort bounds. While the SCP is identified as its own separate entity, there is still the sense of it being her body, allowing her primary jurisdiction over it (there's a reason I made the "host" an SCP researcher, meaning that she can be in control of and report most of the data herself).

I acknowledge and agree with your aside - I had failed to take the publication date into reference - and to answer the hypothetical question at the end, yes, I think I am capable of composing this piece in a way that it does not come off as a joke about the female anatomy, but rather as a respectful commentary on harassment with a twist of sweet vengeance towards misogynists. I will be sure to be careful with my wording and have several people check over it prior to anywhere near potential publication.

With all that in mind, I would be absolutely thrilled if you could read through this again with this new context and provide further commentary! If not, I have already taken up plenty of your time discussing these matters. Thank you yet again for talking this through with me!!

DISCLAIMER: I am a newbie and I can't give green-lights.
Take my advice with a large grain of salt.

I'm leaving this here temporarily, I shall add critique below this as soon as I am able to.

Ello there! So there's quite a bit I really enjoy about this, and then there is some stuff I'd like to give advice on.

I'll start off with what I thought was really good about this concept.

1. I really love how your SCP is setup, it's simple and to the point. It makes it really easy to come across and understand.

2. I also really like the concept, it's one that can lead to a lot when it comes to storytelling of the Foundation staff or people around the SCP. The fact that the SCP moves between different places with not many restrictions means that your story is not constrained from one part physical world. This means you can add lore and interviews revolving around the SCP from multiple different places. Heck, I'd say go one step further and add some wackiness in there. If the SCP isn't restricted to being in a place like a city, have one of the reported locations that it was found in be something crazy like in the middle of a uninhabited desert.

+ show block
– hide block

Now I do have some things I'd like to address that I'm quite confused on.

1. Try being more specific about how the SCP operates. I especially think you need to give some more detail into the "gas station" part of the SCP itself.

  • What kind of gas station is it? Is it of a specific custom brand or does it change randomly between other gas station brands to help its manipulation?
  • Does the gas station change its products, shape, and pricing based on where it's located or is it the same no matter where it is?
  • Does the SCP have any restrictions to where it changes its location? Can it appear in any part of the world or does it only spawn in areas like cities and common gas-station locations? I get that you described in the findings that the SCP was "never there before" according to the staff researcher, but you got to give more detail into where it "moves between places".

2. How does the Foundation know about these findings? According to your story, the body of the staff member was found, but that doesn't describe to the Foundation what exactly happened.

  • If the Foundation can't find the gas station (since it moves after the mirror is shattered) how does the Foundation know that the staff member was even killed by an anomalous entity?

I recommend giving more explanation into this. Here's some ideas I can give:

  • Have the Foundation ask other staff in the local area of any sudden changes.
  • Have the Foundation spot a correlation between multiple discoveries of the same kind of events.

EDIT: Sorry for typos and bad syntax, I was using a phone earlier when reviewing this.
